props.title: Palmetto
props.initialSlug: Ex-con gets tangled in seductive crime scheme

sections.content: Palmetto stands as a fascinating neo-noir that deliberately channels the sultry atmosphere of classic 1940s crime films like Double Indemnity (1944) and The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946). Starring Woody Harrelson as Harry Barber, a wrongly imprisoned journalist who gets tangled in a femme fatale's kidnapping scheme, the film embraces noir tropes while setting them against the sweaty backdrop of Florida's Gulf Coast. Director Volker Schlöndorff, known for The Tin Drum (1979), brings his European sensibilities to this American crime story, creating an atmosphere thick with betrayal and moral ambiguity.

movies.title: The Last Seduction
movies.slug: Linda Fiorentino stars as one of neo-noir's most manipulative femmes fatales

sections.content: While Palmetto received mixed reviews upon release, it fits into the 1990s neo-noir revival that included gems like The Last Seduction (1994) and Red Rock West (1993). These films updated noir conventions for modern audiences while maintaining the genre's core elements of sexual manipulation, greed, and doomed protagonists. Elisabeth Shue's performance as Rhea Malroux channels the dangerous allure of classic femmes fatales like Barbara Stanwyck, while adding contemporary complexity. SUBHEAD: Florida Noir and Contemporary Crime Films

The film's Florida setting places it in a unique subset of sun-soaked noir, alongside films like Body Heat (1981) and Wild Things (1998). These movies trade noir's traditional rain-slicked streets and dark alleys for tropical heat and coastal corruption. The contrast between paradise-like settings and dark criminal undertones creates a distinctive atmosphere that subverts expectations, much like how To Live and Die in L.A. (1985) used sun-bleached Los Angeles locations to create a new kind of noir aesthetic.
